screens.title: What is Rapid Prototyping?
screens.narratorSegment: Rapid prototyping is the deliberate practice of creating a simple, working version of a single game idea to test whether the mechanic is fun and viable. The key is simplicity: prototypes use minimal art and thin systems so you can run many experiments quickly. Benefits include failing fast, getting clear playtester feedback, reducing wasted effort on art that never fits, and exposing unexpected design limitations. A practical example is testing a new movement feel: instead of building a whole level, you create a flat plane and a cube player, attach a movement script, and run playtests to decide if speed and acceleration feel right. Remember that prototypes are experiments, not final products. Keep scope tiny, record clear acceptance criteria before you build, and iterate on a single variable at a time. A common misconception is to treat prototypes as demos; doing so wastes time on polish. Instead, treat them as controlled tests where measurable changes teach you about your design. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › What is Rapid Prototyping?
Definition

A fast, low-fidelity, playable version that tests the core mechanics and player experience with minimal polish.

Benefits
  • Fail fast and learn what does not work.
  • Save resources by avoiding premature polish.
  • Gather early player feedback on core feel.
  • Test single variables in isolation.
Key Takeaway

Prototypes are experiments. Decide success criteria before you build.

Practical example

Test movement by creating a Player cube, adding a Rigidbody, and attaching a short movement script. Run and adjust speed until it feels right.

Setup
Create Player cube, add Rigidbody, create PlayerMovement script, attach script, press Play.
Measure
Note player speed, responsiveness, and whether the mechanic is fun during short playtests.
Common mistake
Adding art and polish too soon hides whether the mechanic itself is enjoyable.

screens.title: Unity Editor: Core Windows
screens.narratorSegment: The Unity Editor is composed of a few essential windows you will use constantly. The Scene view is your sandbox for placing and arranging objects; you manipulate transforms and visually compose levels there. The Game view shows what the player will see when you press Play, helping you check camera framing and gameplay feel. The Hierarchy lists all GameObjects in the current scene and is the canonical place to select and organize them. The Project window holds assets stored on disk, such as scripts, prefabs, and materials. Finally, the Inspector displays properties and components of the selected object, where you add components like Rigidbody, Collider, or custom scripts. Knowing the responsibilities of each window speeds up iteration: create a cube in the Hierarchy, inspect it to add a Rigidbody, then tune values and press Play in the Game view to test. A frequent novice error is looking for assets in the Scene instead of the Project window; remember that Scene shows instances while Project stores persistent files. screens.title: GameObject and Components
screens.narratorSegment: In Unity, everything you place in a scene is a GameObject. A GameObject alone is an empty container; it gains functionality when you attach Components. The Transform component is present on every GameObject and defines its position, rotation, and scale in the scene. To make a cube physically simulated, add a Rigidbody component—this allows gravity, forces, and collisions to affect the object. A Collider defines the physical boundary for collisions; choose a Box Collider for a cube. When you check Is Trigger on a Collider, the object no longer physically blocks others but will still send trigger events. Combining these components is how Unity composes behavior without inheritance-heavy class trees. A common beginner mistake is forgetting to add a Rigidbody when expecting physics interactions. Another is leaving the Collider unchecked as a trigger when you wanted event detection rather than physical blocking. In rapid prototyping, primitives plus the right components let you simulate gameplay quickly without custom geometry or art. GameObject and Components means attach components to gameobjects—transform for position, rigidbody for physics, collider for collisions or triggers.. In practical terms, how transform, rigidbody, and collider combine to make behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

GameObject basics

GameObjects are containers. Add components to give them behavior and appearance.

Transform
Position, rotation, and scale are always present and used to place objects in the scene.
Rigidbody
Enables physics simulation so objects fall and respond to forces.
Collider
Defines the collision volume. Use Is Trigger for event-only interactions.
Example: Player cube

Create a cube named Player, add a Rigidbody and a Box Collider. Tag it as Player in the Inspector for script checks.

  • Rigidbody component added.

screens.title: C# Scripting Basics in Unity
screens.narratorSegment: C# is Unity’s primary scripting language and it uses a component model: a script is a component you attach to a GameObject. Typical scripts include Start, which runs once when the component is enabled, and Update, which runs every frame. Public variables declared in a script appear in the Inspector so designers can tweak values without changing code. Time. deltaTime represents the time since the last frame and is essential for frame-rate independent movement. A simple movement script reads horizontal input, constructs a movement vector, and applies it multiplied by speed and Time. deltaTime. Common mistakes include forgetting to save the script, not attaching it to the GameObject, or missing the Time. deltaTime factor which causes movement speed to vary across hardware. When prototyping, keep scripts short and focused. Attach the script to your Player cube, tune moveSpeed in the Inspector, and use the Console to check for errors if behavior is not as expected. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › C# Scripting Basics
Key script parts
  • Start() runs once on enable for initialization.
  • Update() runs each frame for input and movement.
  • public fields show in Inspector for tuning.
  • Time.deltaTime makes movement frame-rate independent.
Pro-tip
Expose speeds and thresholds as public fields so playtesters can tune without recompiling code.
Starter code
<!-- PlayerMovement.cs -->
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerMovement : MonoBehaviour
{
  public float moveSpeed = 5f; // Adjust in Inspector

  void Update()
  {
    float horizontalInput = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
    Vector3 movement = new Vector3(horizontalInput, 0f, 0f);
    transform.Translate(movement * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime);
  }
}
Save the script, then drag it onto the Player cube or use Add Component to attach it. Tune moveSpeed and press Play to test motion.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › PlayerMovement Script Explained
Script details
<!-- PlayerMovement.cs -->
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerMovement : MonoBehaviour
{
  public float moveSpeed = 5f; // Public variable to adjust speed in the Inspector

  void Update()
  {
    // Get horizontal input (e.g., A/D keys or Left/Right arrow keys)
    float horizontalInput = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");

    // Calculate movement direction
    Vector3 movement = new Vector3(horizontalInput, 0f, 0f);

    // Move the GameObject
    transform.Translate(movement * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime);
  }
}
Input.GetAxis
Returns smoothed input for left/right controls mapped to Horizontal.
Time.deltaTime
Delta time keeps movement consistent across varying frame rates.
Example scenario

using UnityEngine;

public class GoalTrigger : MonoBehaviour
{

screens.title: Prototype vs Polished Build
screens.narratorSegment: A prototype and a polished build serve different goals and should be treated differently. A prototype focuses on answering a single question quickly: does a mechanic feel good, or does an interaction work? It uses simple assets, minimal systems, and short, testable scripts. A polished build, in contrast, is meant for release: finished art, full systems, and extensive testing. The danger is polishing too early. Investing in graphics and complex systems before the mechanic is proven wastes time if the core idea fails. For example, if you are experimenting with a sprint-and-slide mechanic, prototype with a cube and basic forces to validate the feel. Only after multiple successful playtests should you replace the cube with a character model and add animations. Prototyping lets you run more experiments per week. screens.title: Common Errors and Debugging
screens.narratorSegment: Debugging in Unity often starts with the Console window. When a script fails to compile, Unity shows errors in the Console and the offending script will not run. Read error messages from top to bottom: they usually include file and line numbers. If a runtime behavior is missing, add Debug. Log statements in Start, Update, or event handlers to confirm code execution. Frequent beginner errors in prototyping include disabled components or GameObjects, missing Rigidbody when expecting physics or triggers, and incorrect tags used in CompareTag checks. Another common issue is forgetting to save the script in your code editor so Unity never sees changes. For physics-related checks, remember FixedUpdate is the timing target for physics, while Update handles per-frame input. Finally, replicate the problem in a minimal scene to isolate the issue: remove unrelated components and test only the Player and Goal. Rapid prototyping is the practice of building a simple, playable version of a game idea so you can test whether it feels fun before committing time and art. In Unity, you can assemble primitive shapes, attach physics, and write a few lines of C# to verify a mechanic in hours instead of weeks. This chapter shows you how to use the Unity Editor’s core windows, create basic GameObjects, add components like Rigidbody and Collider, and write minimal scripts for player movement and goal detection. A prototype and a polished build serve different goals and should be treated differently. A prototype focuses on answering a single question quickly: does a mechanic feel good, or does an interaction work? It uses simple assets, minimal systems, and short, testable scripts. A polished build, in contrast, is meant for release: finished art, full systems, and extensive testing. The danger is polishing too early. Investing in graphics and complex systems before the mechanic is proven wastes time if the core idea fails. For example, if you are experimenting with a sprint-and-slide mechanic, prototype with a cube and basic forces to validate the feel. Only after multiple successful playtests should you replace the cube with a character model and add animations. Prototyping lets you run more experiments per week. Polishing is done once the high-risk design choices are resolved. Keep acceptance criteria clear so you know when to stop prototyping and begin polish.
